stances.claim: Edsa 1 and Edsa 2, though similar in methods (peaceful assemblies, military and Church support) and outcomes (presidential ousting and women's elevation), were justified by the SC on contrasting doctrinal grounds -- Edsa 1 as extra-constitutional revolution (Lawyers League v. Aquino's non-justiciability ruling because the 1973 Constitution was obliterated) and Edsa 2 as intra-constitutional exercise of freedom of speech and assembly preserving the 1987 Constitution (Estrada v. Desierto's 13-0 ruling).
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-contrast-by-verbatim-citation (using SC's own words in 406 Phil 1, 44)

stances.claim: The fading observance of both Edsa anniversaries -- even by Arroyo herself sub silentio -- is the symptom of Edsa's over-identification with partisan political groups (Edsa 1 with the Liberal Party and Aquino family, Edsa 2 with Arroyo and her regime), making the celebrations a function of partisan victory rather than democratic memory.

Edsa should be depoliticized -- shorn of partisan color and accepted as the Filipino nation's supreme contribution to democracy's intrepid journey, as momentous as the British Magna Carta and the American Declaration of Independence, belonging to the nation rather than to Cory, Gloria, or any clan or leader.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative-historical-elevation (placing Edsa alongside Magna Carta and Declaration)

stances.claim: Duterte's hailing of Edsa as 'enduring proof that history can be rewritten without the need to resort to violent means' -- despite his skipping the personal appearance -- is a vital milestone in the depoliticization process, because a non-Aquino, non-Arroyo president affirming Edsa breaks the partisan capture pattern.
stances.rhetorical_move: unlikely-affirmer-as-depoliticization-evidence (Duterte's distance from the Edsa coalitions makes his affirmation more legitimizing)

notable_anecdotes: CJ's personal disclosure that he and CJ Davide inhibited from Estrada v. Desierto (March 2, 2001) -- making the 13-0 vote rather than 15-0 -- anchoring the column's doctrinal analysis in CJ's first-person institutional experience.

The verbatim SC quotation from Estrada v. Desierto (406 Phil 1, 44) preserved in CJ's column -- 'EDSA I is extra constitutional... EDSA II is intra constitutional... EDSA I presented a political question; EDSA II involves legal questions' -- used as the column's doctrinal centerpiece.

Arroyo ignoring her own ascendant moment 'sub silentio' during her presidency -- the most quietly devastating fact in the column, since the very beneficiary chose silence on the event that made her president.
Duterte hailing Edsa 'while skipping personal appearance' -- the dual-signal of substantive endorsement plus physical absence that CJ reads as a step toward depoliticization rather than as a slight.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban contrasts the Supreme Court's doctrinal justifications for the two People Power revolutions: Edsa 1 (February 22-25, 1986), which Lawyers League v. Aquino (May 22, 1986) treated as non-justiciable because the 1973 Constitution had been obliterated by the revolution itself, and Edsa 2 (January 16-20, 2001), which Estrada v. Desierto (March 2, 2001, 13-0 with CJ Davide and Panganiban inhibited) treated as intra-constitutional -- an exercise of freedom of speech and assembly within the still-existing 1987 Constitution, producing a presidential resignation and vice-presidential succession subject to judicial review. He quotes the SC verbatim: 'EDSA I is extra constitutional... EDSA II is intra constitutional... EDSA I presented a political question; EDSA II involves legal questions.' He then laments the fading observance of both anniversaries -- even by Arroyo herself sub silentio -- diagnosing the cause as Edsa's over-identification with partisan groups: Edsa 1 with the Liberal Party and the Aquino family, Edsa 2 with Arroyo and her regime. He calls for depoliticization, urging that Edsa be 'shorn of partisan political color and accepted as our people's supreme contribution to democracy's intrepid journey, as momentous as the British Magna Carta and the American Declaration of Independence.' He reads Duterte's rhetorical affirmation (despite skipping personal appearance) -- that Edsa is enduring proof history can be rewritten without violence -- as a vital depoliticization milestone, precisely because a non-Aquino, non-Arroyo president's endorsement breaks the partisan-capture pattern. He closes: 'Cory, Gloria and their partisans do not own Edsa. Indeed, People Power belongs to the Filipino nation, not to any partisan political group or clan or leader.'
